title: OET Reading Practice Test 2
instructions: OET Reading has three parts. Part A: rapid reading across short healthcare texts. Part B: short workplace texts. Part C: two longer healthcare texts. Choose the best answer for each question.

parts.title: Part A — Expeditious Reading
parts.description: Four short texts on a single healthcare topic; locate specific information quickly.

parts.title: Part B — Workplace Texts
parts.description: Short workplace documents (policies, manuals, notices); one multiple-choice question each.

parts.title: Part C — Presentation of Opinion
parts.description: Two long texts; detailed comprehension of opinion, attitude and argument.

passages.title: Text A: Recognising hypoglycaemia
passages.text: Hypoglycaemia is defined as a blood glucose level below 4.0 mmol/L. Early autonomic symptoms include sweating, tremor, palpitations and hunger; these arise from adrenaline release and usually give the patient warning. Neuroglycopenic symptoms — confusion, slurred speech, drowsiness, behavioural change — appear as glucose falls further and indicate that the brain itself is deprived. Patients with long-standing diabetes may develop impaired awareness, losing the autonomic warning stage entirely and presenting first with confusion. Always confirm with a capillary glucose reading before treating, unless the patient is unconscious and delay would be dangerous.

passages.title: Text B: Treating the conscious patient
passages.text: For a conscious patient able to swallow, give 15 to 20 grams of fast-acting carbohydrate: 150 mL of pure fruit juice, five glucose tablets, or four to five jelly babies. Chocolate is not suitable, as its fat content slows absorption. Recheck the capillary glucose after 15 minutes and repeat the treatment if the level remains below 4.0 mmol/L. Once above 4.0, give a long-acting carbohydrate such as two biscuits or a slice of toast to prevent recurrence, unless the patient is about to eat a meal or is receiving a continuous feed.

passages.title: Text C: The unconscious or uncooperative patient
passages.text: Never give oral carbohydrate to a patient who is unconscious or unable to protect their airway. If intravenous access is available, administer 100 mL of 20% glucose over 15 minutes; if not, give 1 mg glucagon intramuscularly. Glucagon works by mobilising hepatic glycogen and will therefore be ineffective in a malnourished patient, in advanced liver disease, or where alcohol is the precipitant. Place the patient in the recovery position and recheck glucose after 10 minutes. Once conscious and able to swallow, follow with long-acting carbohydrate as for the conscious patient.

passages.title: Text D: Preventing recurrence
passages.text: Every episode requires a documented review of its cause before the patient is discharged or handed over. Common precipitants are a missed or delayed meal, an unusual amount of exercise, excess alcohol, and an insulin or sulfonylurea dose that no longer matches the patient's intake. Review the timing of insulin against meals rather than simply reducing the dose. Patients experiencing recurrent episodes, or those with impaired awareness, should be referred to the diabetes specialist team; impaired awareness can often be reversed by scrupulously avoiding hypoglycaemia for several weeks.

passages.title: Mental Health Assessment Protocol
passages.text: All patients presenting to the emergency department with behavioural changes must receive a brief mental health screening within one hour of arrival. Assessment should include current mood, suicidal or homicidal ideation, substance use, and recent stressors. Patients expressing suicidal intent must be placed under continuous observation on a one-to-one basis. A psychiatry liaison team should be consulted within two hours for high-risk cases. All assessments must be documented thoroughly with patient quotes where possible. Discharge planning for psychiatric patients must include community support arrangements and follow-up appointments before leaving the hospital.

passages.title: Blood Transfusion Safety Checklist
passages.text: Before administering blood products, ensure patient identity is verified using two identifiers. Check that the blood unit label matches the patient's blood type and antibody screen results. Inspect the blood bag for discolouration, gas bubbles, or any signs of contamination; if found, return to the blood bank immediately. Baseline vital signs must be recorded before transfusion starts. During transfusion, observe for adverse reactions including fever, chills, rash, or shortness of breath. Vital signs should be checked at 15 minutes and 1 hour; if any reaction occurs, stop transfusion immediately and inform the physician.

passages.title: Pressure Injury Prevention and Management
passages.text: Pressure injuries, formerly known as pressure ulcers or bedsores, are localised injuries to the skin and underlying tissue resulting from sustained pressure. These injuries are largely preventable through systematic assessment and intervention. Risk factors include immobility, poor nutrition, incontinence, and advanced age. The Braden Scale is the most widely used risk assessment tool, scoring factors such as sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction. Patients scoring moderate to high risk require intensive prevention strategies including regular repositioning every two hours, use of pressure-relieving mattresses and cushions, meticulous skin care, adequate nutrition, and management of incontinence. Early recognition is crucial: Stage 1 involves non-blanching redness over a bony prominence; Stage 2 includes partial-thickness skin loss with a pink wound bed; Stage 3 represents full-thickness skin loss; Stage 4 involves tissue necrosis. Reverse staging is not recommended as it does not reflect healing. Treatment depends on wound characteristics and may include topical agents, dressings, debridement, and occasionally surgery. Prevention is always superior to treatment, and systems audits of facility-acquired injuries guide quality improvement initiatives.

passages.title: Diabetes Self-Management Education
passages.text: Effective diabetes management requires patients to understand their condition and take active responsibility for daily care. Structured education programmes have been shown to reduce HbA1c levels by up to 1.5% and decrease complications. Key educational topics include recognising hypoglycaemic symptoms such as tremor, sweating, and confusion, and carrying fast-acting carbohydrates at all times. Patients on insulin must learn proper injection technique and rotate injection sites to prevent lipodystrophy. Blood glucose monitoring frequency depends on medication type: insulin users should test four times daily, whilst those on oral agents may test less frequently if glucose targets are met. Dietary advice should focus on carbohydrate awareness, portion control, and regular meal timing rather than restrictive dieting. Physical activity of at least 150 minutes per week at moderate intensity is recommended. Emotional well-being is critical as depression and anxiety increase diabetes complications; psychological support should be offered routinely. Patients should learn foot care including daily inspection, appropriate footwear, and prompt reporting of any sores. Annual complications screening includes eye assessment for retinopathy, urine albumin testing for nephropathy, and monofilament testing for neuropathy. Empowering patients through education reduces hospitalisations and improves quality of life.
